newsitem.title: USA: U.S. hopes for deal with Japan on port row.
newsitem.headline: U.S. hopes for deal with Japan on port row.

text.p: A U.S.-Japan agreement in a dispute over access to Japanese ports is still uncertain as a deadline for imposing U.S. sanctions looms, State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said on Friday.
But a senior official, speaking on condition of anonymity, was more upbeat. "The talks are going okay. We hope for an agreement" this weekend, the official said.
Burns, at a news briefing, said both sides "obviously want an agreement (but) it's hard to predict where we're going to come out today."

Officials said privately that the talks, taking place in Washington, would probably continue over the weekend as the U.S. side, at least, was keen to conclude them before Monday, the U.S. deadline for sanctions.

On that day, the U.S. Federal Maritime Commission has said it will impose penalties of $100,000 per visit on Japanese carriers calling at American ports if Tokyo does not move quickly to open access to Japenese ports.
The United States contends its shipping firms are treated unfairly by Tokyo, which maintains tight controls on the licensing of stevedores and port operaitons in Japan.
U.S. firms want to be able to hire their own stevedores and set up their own operations, claiming they could save money and improve productivity.
Burns signalled that Washington wants to be able to conclude the negotiations by Monday.

"We have said that if there no action by Monday, April 14, the Federal Maritime Commission will be forced to charge Japanese liners $100,000 if they visit our ports because there have been discriminatory practices against our own liners."
The penalties were imposed by the commission in February after the two countries failed to resolve the five-year-old dispute.
